1:
Job breaks his long silence not with an answer to his friends but with a groan wrung from his own weariness, and the witnesses gather first around what it means to be "weary of my life" and where a sufferer may lawfully leave his complaint. The reformed John Gill catalogues the weariness by what it is not: not the weariness of a guilty conscience pressed by the horror of sin, as with Cain or Judas, nor the holy longing of a Paul to be dissolved and rid of indwelling corruption, nor grief at the sins of others; it is simply that Job, his body one continual sore, would not live always and was uneasy to dwell any longer in his earthly tabernacle. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on the noun for "soul" as a small doctrinal treasure: nephesh here is not the animal life (that is chai) but the immortal mind, proof that Job was no materialist but credited the soul's proper immortality.

On the middle clause the schools genuinely diverge. Clarke reads "I will leave my complaint upon myself" as a vow of self-blame: "I still charge myself with the cause of my own calamities, and shall not charge my Maker foolishly." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the opposite, not the leaving of blame on himself but "I will give free vent to the complaint that is upon me," comparing the outburst of the previous chapter. So the very words that Clarke and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry read as Job's refusal to impeach God, Ellicott takes as the loosing of a torrent.

Henry weighs the whole resolution with a pastor's care. Daunted by the dread of God's majesty so that he cannot plead his cause, Job resolves to ease himself by giving vent to his resentments, "fallen out with life, and sick of it." Through the weakness of grace, Henry owns, he went contrary to the dictates of nature itself, for faith and patience would have kept him from being weary of his life. Yet grace still puts in a word: Job will not give vent by violent hands but only by violent words, and "it shall be the bitterness of his soul that he will express, not his settled judgment"; if he speaks amiss, it is not his soul but its bitterness. John Wesley catches the same hesitation in the bare question that opens the Hebrew, "Shall I give over complaining?" The witnesses converge on a sufferer resolved to speak, and part only over whether that speech is a confession that shoulders the blame or a complaint at last set free.
2:
Turning from resolve to actual address, Job frames the first petition of his speech, "Do not condemn me; shew me wherefore thou contendest with me," and the witnesses read it as a prayer at once bold and reverent. The reformed John Gill is careful that "condemn me" cannot mean eternal condemnation, for to those in Christ there is none; the force is rather "do not account me wicked," do not treat me as an abandoned sinner by prolonging this stroke, since God himself knew Job was not the man his friends supposed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the pair of lines together, "I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. I will say to Eloah: Condemn me not; let me know wherefore Thou contendest with me!" In them they find the cry of a self-consciousness that longs to answer for itself: weary of life and asking nothing for its continuance, Job begs only that the Author of his sufferings not let him die the death of the wicked against the testimony of his own conscience.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press both halves. Adam Clarke glosses "do not condemn me" as "let me not be afflicted in thy wrath," and lays down his settled maxim on the second clause: "God never afflicts but for past sin, or to try his followers, or for the greater manifestation of his grace" in their support and deliverance; so if sin be the cause, let it be named. John Wesley reads the request for a vindication: "pronounce me not to be a wicked man, neither deal with me as such; O discover my integrity by removing this stroke, for which my friends condemn me." The "wherefore," Wesley adds, asks for what ends and for what sins, since Job is "not conscious of any peculiar sins by which I have deserved to be made the most miserable of all men."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lifts the verse above Job's particular case and makes it a pattern for every believer: here is "a model of prayer for all," combining the publican's cry of Luke 18:13 with that longing for light which the soul feels most keenly in seasons of affliction and darkness. The witnesses do not divide over the substance. They agree that Job neither denies God's right to correct nor confesses a hidden wickedness; he asks only two things, that the correction not be the sentence of a condemning Judge, and that its reason be made known, and Wesley draws the abiding lesson, that when God contends with us there is always a reason, and it is our wisdom to learn what it is that we may forsake whatever he has a controversy with us for.
3:
The petition hardens into expostulation as Job asks whether it can be "good" to God to "oppress" and to "despise the work of thine hands," and the witnesses feel the boldness of the question even as they trace its logic. The reformed John Gill will not soften it: this and what follows are "expostulations too bold and daring," in which Job uses too much freedom with the Almighty. Yet Gill grants the premise on which the boldness rests, that God dehorts men from oppression, threatens to punish it, and rises to help the oppressed, and so will never delight in it himself; Job's error is only in supposing that his afflictions are such an oppression, and that God took some seeming pleasure in pressing hard upon him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke unfolds the three clauses as one indictment framed in astonishment. It can be "no gratification" to God to distress the children of men, "as if thou didst despise the work of thy own hands"; and the last clause, to "shine upon the counsel of the wicked," Clarke reads as Job's sharpest fear, that by his sufferings the harsh verdict of the ungodly seems confirmed, namely that God regards not his most fervent worshippers, so that there is no benefit in leading a religious life. The stroke that falls on the righteous man appears to light up, as with approval, the very argument of the profane.

John Wesley, also wesleyan-arminian, keeps the reverent restraint that Gill demands. "Is it good" means "Dost thou take any pleasure in it?" and Wesley is quick to add the guard: "Far be it from Job to think that God did him wrong." The difficulty is not that Job accuses God of injustice but that he "is at a loss to reconcile his providences with his justice," a perplexity, Wesley observes, in which other good men have often been, and will be, until the day shall declare it. So the witnesses hold two things together without collapsing either: the words are dangerously free, pushing hard against the goodness of God, and yet they are the words of a man who cannot bring himself to charge his Maker with wrong, only to cry out that oppression, contempt of his own handiwork, and the countenancing of the wicked are things utterly unbecoming the God he still trusts. What looks like a challenge to divine justice is, at bottom, the bafflement of a faith that cannot yet see how the frown on God's face agrees with the love it knows to be in his heart.
4:
"Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth?" Job's question turns on the gulf between divine and human sight, and the witnesses expound it as a denial that God could ever be mistaken about a man. The reformed John Gill draws out the contrast at length: God has eyes indeed, of love and mercy toward his people, of displeasure toward sinners, but not fleshly ones. Eyes of flesh cannot see at any distance, cannot see in the dark, take in one object at a time, and are at last deceived and fail; but the eyes of God behold all the children of men at once, pierce the darkness as the light, and read the very hearts that outward looks conceal. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts the whole verse in a sentence, "Dost thou judge as man judges?" the second line only illustrating the first.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the question at the head of the great passage that follows on the making of man, noting that the mystery of the embryo's forming was reckoned by the Hebrew wisdom one of the deepest of all secrets, a wonder they range beside Ecclesiastes 11:5. The point of Job's question, on their reading, is that the God who framed man so intimately cannot need to peer or probe as a man would.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the argument into its edge against the divine scrutiny Job feels himself under. God, he says, does not discover things nor judge of them as men do, for he has not eyes of flesh; being a Spirit, he is not confined to one place, nor wearied so that his sight decays, nor liable to the illusions of sense. Men judge at best "according to what is alleged and proved," by the thing as it appears rather than as it is, and too often by the bias of their interests and prejudices; but the judgment of God is according to truth, for he tries the heart and knows it not by information but by his own inspection. The sting of the verse, all the witnesses feel, is that Job means it to reproach the way God is dealing with him: if the Almighty sees so perfectly, why does he handle a man he knows to be no hypocrite as though he had to search out a hidden guilt? The question that magnifies God's knowledge is bent, in Job's mouth, into a complaint that such knowledge should seem to inquire at all.
5:
Job presses the same disproportion from sight to time, asking whether God's "days" and "years" can be "as the days of man," and the witnesses read it as an argument from eternity against the need for any drawn-out inquest. The reformed John Gill answers the rhetorical question flatly: they are not, not so few, for a thousand years with the Lord are but as one day; and not so changeable, for the God who is of one mind is not, like man, of one mind today and another tomorrow. Job's afflictions, Gill allows, might tempt him to think otherwise, as if a God who smiled one day and stripped him the next had altered; but the dispensations change while the divine nature and purpose do not.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the two Hebrew words for "man" and finds a deliberate gradation. The first, enosh, is wretched, mortal man; the second, gaber, the strong man in his vigour; and neither can be measured against God. Man in his low estate cannot be likened to the Eternal, nor even man at his best, made in God's own image; not the longest-lived patriarch's years come near the years of God, a difference of phraseology, Clarke insists, that the sense requires.

John Wesley draws out the practical force of the contrast for the argument Job is building. Man's time is short and uncertain, and so a human judge must hurry, "diligently search out the crimes of malefactors, lest by death he lose the opportunity of doing justice"; but God is eternal, and "seest at one view all men's hearts, and all their actions present and to come." Therefore, Wesley has Job reason, God has no need to proceed against a sufferer in this protracted way, "by making so long a scrutiny into my heart and life." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry read the couplet to the same end: unlike men, to whom truth is the daughter of time and who grow wiser only by slow experience and repeated trial, God is not short-lived, and to him nothing is past or future but everything present. The witnesses do not divide. They hear in the verse a single reproachful inference, that the long, examining severity Job feels would suit a mortal magistrate racing against his own death, but sits strangely on a God whose one glance is eternity, and who therefore cannot need to torture a confession out of time.
6:
The two previous questions come to their point here, in the clause they were built to carry: "that thou enquirest after mine iniquity, and searchest after my sin." The reformed John Gill reads the searching as a relentless audit, God narrowly examining every action of Job's life to find something amiss, taking notice of every weakness, watching every halting, as though he must have some charge to justify the affliction. Worse, Gill says, it is a dealing that proceeds "as if there was no Messiah, no Mediator, Redeemer, and Saviour provided," and no forgiveness of sin through him; for sin pardoned is covered so that when it is sought it cannot be found, whereas here it seems laid open and searched out for punishment. Job imagined, Gill adds, that the very design of his afflictions was to put him on the rack and so extort a confession.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the indignity into a single question: "Is it becoming thy infinite dignity to concern thyself so much with the affairs or transgressions of a despicable mortal?" a word, he notes drily, that has passed through the heart of most sinners. John Wesley reduces the complaint to the image that governs it, "keeping me so long upon the rack, to compel me to accuse myself." The searching, on both readings, is not a discovery, for the all-seeing and eternal God of v.4 and v.5 can need none, but a torment, a slow pressure meant to wring out an admission that Job does not believe he owes at all.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry ties the strangeness of it to the honour of God himself. That God should prolong the torture, neither bringing his sufferer to trial nor granting release, wears an aspect "dishonourable to God, and would tempt men to think him a hard master." Henry will not let Job be understood to charge God with actually needing to hunt out his sin; rather Job pleads with God to consider his own great name: "if thou wilt not consult my comfort, consult thy own honour; do something for thy great name," as the prophet prayed in Jeremiah 14:21. So the witnesses converge on the burden of the verse, that the endless inquest into a known man's guilt befits neither the omniscience nor the eternity nor the goodness just ascribed to God, and that Job, unable to reconcile it, throws the difficulty back upon God's own care for his glory.
7:
The argument reaches its boldest ground in Job's appeal to God's own knowledge, "Thou knowest that I am not wicked," set against the helplessness of the last clause, "there is none that can deliver out of thine hand." The reformed John Gill is careful to fix what the claim does and does not assert. Job does not pretend to be sinless; he has already owned himself a sinner and guilty before God. What he protests is that he is not the wicked man, the hypocrite, his friends read in his sufferings, that sin has not had the dominion over him, that he has not secretly cherished some reigning iniquity; and for the truth of this he can appeal to the Searcher of hearts, the very God who yet pursues him as though he were guilty.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke frames it as a wounded question: while thou hast this perfect knowledge of me and my conduct, "why appear to be sifting me as if in order to find out sin," and treat me as a transgressor when none can be found? John Wesley reads "wicked" the same way, "an hypocrite, as my friends account me," and then turns to the darker second clause, where Job bows even as he protests: since God is the supreme ruler and none can wrest a prisoner from his hand, "I must wait thy time, and throw myself on thy mercy, in submission to thy sovereign will."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a fine adjustment to the plea, hearing in it less a boast of innocence than a forensic hope: the meaning is rather "that I shall not be found guilty," not the confident appeal of a Peter in John 21:17, but the language the Psalmist would afterward borrow when he prayed to the God whose hands had made him in Psalm 119:73. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the comfort the verse hides beneath its complaint. It is to no purpose to contend with Omnipotence, and that is what should quiet us under trouble; but what abundantly comforts is to be able to say with Job, "Lord, thou knowest that I am not wicked," for "thou knowest I love thee." So the witnesses turn the verse two ways at once: outward, as a protest that a God of perfect sight cannot honestly reckon Job a hypocrite; and inward, as the deep rest of a man who, unable to escape the hand that grips him, can yet lay his integrity open before the very eyes that hold him fast.
8:
"Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost destroy me." With these words Job turns from the courtroom to the workshop, and the witnesses follow him into a long plea grounded on his own creation. The reformed John Gill reads the whole movement as designed to move God to pity: not Job himself, nor even his parents, but God only had made him, a curious piece wrought by the hands of divine power and wisdom; and the God whose hands so framed a man has surely a claim of tenderness upon the work he alone can either keep or unmake. Gill checks one over-reading, that "hands" should be pressed into a distinct reference to the Son and the Spirit, as a strain the words will not bear, though he does not exclude the whole Godhead from the making of man.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the craftsmanship the Hebrew names. God has "refined the materials" and modified them into an exquisite symmetry, so that both the union and harmony of the parts (yachad) and their arrangement and completion (sabib) proclaim his skill; and against all that skill stands the terrible verb, which Clarke renders "and thou wilt swallow me up." Men prize most the works on which they have spent the most pains, "yet thou art about to destroy me"; and Clarke draws from the paradox how dreadful an evil sin must be, that on its account so curiously fashioned a body must be decomposed to dust. Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, render the couplet with the same shock, "Thy hands have formed and perfected me altogether round about, and Thou hast now swallowed me up!"

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse the opening of a sustained argument from being. God made us, and not we ourselves; his hands have made and fashioned these bodies of ours, fearfully and wonderfully. And this creaturely dependence Henry turns straight into a plea: "Thou hast made me, and therefore thou hast a perfect knowledge of me, and needest not to examine me by scourging"; "thou hast made me as the clay by an act of sovereignty, and wilt thou by a like act unmake me again?" It is the plea of the saints, "we are the clay, and thou our potter," echoing the appeal of Isaiah 64:8 and the confession of Psalm 119:73. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the verse the ache of a workmanship that cannot understand why its own Maker should turn to destroy it, and the confidence that the very hands which formed a man are the likeliest of all to spare him.
9:
The plea of the potter and the clay now becomes explicit, "Remember that thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again?" and the witnesses weigh both the likeness and the pathos of the appeal. The reformed John Gill asks in what sense man is "as the clay," and answers that it is not the impurity of clay that is meant, for God made man upright, but its brittleness: as a vessel of clay is easily broken and cannot bear a heavy stroke, so the body of man is a frail thing, and Job pleads that frailty as itself a reason God should not press so hard. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the reproach folded into the question: God has fashioned man out of a mass of clay with such skill and pains that men might well suppose themselves made for a permanent being, "but thou hast decreed to turn them into dust!"

John Wesley finds two distinct arguments in the single image. The clay speaks of "the frailty of man's nature, which of itself decays and perishes, and doth not need such violent shocks to overthrow it," a broken vessel needing no smashing; and it speaks too of "the excellency of the Divine artifice," commended the more from the meanness of the materials, which is itself a plea why God should not destroy so fine a thing wrought from so poor a stuff. And Wesley hears in "wilt thou bring me into dust again" the concession that softens the whole: "I must die by the course of nature, and therefore while I do live, give me some ease and comfort."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott anchors the return to dust in its scriptural echo, comparing the wasted strength of Psalm 22:15, where the sufferer is brought to the dust of death; and Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain force of the plea, that the God who made him as clay is besought to remember it before he crumbles it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the "remember" into the heart of a saint's prayer: "Thou madest me, and knowest my strength; wilt thou then suffer me to be pressed above measure? Wilt thou destroy the work of thy own hands?" If we plead our creation with ourselves as a motive to duty, God made me, therefore I will serve him, we may plead it with God as an argument for mercy: "Thou hast made me; do thou new-make me; I am thine, save me." The witnesses agree that the verse is not a denial of mortality but a claim upon the Maker's compassion, drawn from the very dust to which man must one day return.
10:
"Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?" Job carries the making of man back to its hidden beginning, and the witnesses divide gently over what exactly the two images describe. The reformed John Gill takes the verse to express, "in modest terms," the conception of a man from the seed of his parents, a matter compared to milk both for being a liquid and for its colour. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke argues the point strongly and settles it on generation rather than mere nourishment: after all that learned men have written to confine the figure to nutrition, he is satisfied that the verse looks to the first forming of the embryo in the womb, coalescing from the seed of both parents; the pouring out like milk, the curdling into shape, the clothing with flesh and the fencing with bones that follow, all "well imagined, and delicately, and at the same time forcibly, expressed."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees in a word, calling the poured-out milk "an allusion to the embryo," and sending the reader to the kindred wonder of the Psalmist who was woven in the lowest parts of the earth in Psalm 139:13. John Wesley dwells on the delicacy and the exactness of the picture together: the verse "modestly and accurately describes God's admirable work in making man out of a small and liquid, and as it were milky substance, by degrees congealed and condensed into that exquisite frame of man's body," the whole marvel of gestation compressed into the homely images of the dairy.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the line as one clause of an elegant description of how human bodies are formed in the womb, "poured out like milk, which is coagulated into cheese," and then set forward by the induction of particulars in the verse that follows. What all the witnesses feel is the strange tenderness of the argument: Job is not merely describing embryology but pressing a plea, reminding God of the extraordinary care and artistry lavished on him before he ever drew breath. The God who took such pains to bring a man from a drop to a living frame is being asked, by the very intimacy of that work, why he should now undo it. The images are gentle, almost domestic; but under them runs the same hard question that drives the whole speech, why so wonderful a beginning should end in a swallowing-up. The mystery of the womb becomes, in Job's mouth, an appeal against the mystery of his ruin.
11:
The forming of the embryo now advances to the finished body, "Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews," and the witnesses admire the order and the artistry the verse records. The reformed John Gill takes the two verbs as marking two garments: the bones clothed with flesh as an inner garment, the flesh with skin as the outer, a covering he calls artificially composed of arteries, veins, nerves, glands, and innumerable pores so fine that a multitude of them might be covered by a single grain of sand. He notes the order of generation the verse seems to observe, the inward parts first consolidated, then the outward flesh and skin drawn over them for defence; and he even lifts the image to a higher clothing, the righteousness of the living Redeemer with which Job's soul was clad.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same gradual method: God "covered my inward and more noble parts, which are first formed," and so proceeds step by step in the making of a man; the bones he calls "the stay and strength of the body," some of them, the skull and the ribs, set to enclose and defend its vital organs. The verse, on his reading, is a catalogue of provisions, each part fashioned with a use in view.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the picture into a single figure of clothing and armour. Though we come into the world naked, he says, the body is itself both clothed and armed: "the skin and flesh are its clothing; the bones and sinews are its armour, not offensive, but defensive." The vital parts, the heart and lungs, are thus clothed so as not to be seen and fenced so as not to be hurt; and this admirable structure of the human body is "an illustrious instance of the wisdom, power, and goodness of the Creator." Henry cannot forbear the moral pressed upon such a frame: "what a pity is it that these bodies should be instruments of unrighteousness which are capable of being temples of the Holy Ghost!" The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain rendering, "clothed me with skin and flesh, and fenced me with bones and sinews," letting the anatomy speak for itself as one more clause in the great argument from creation. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as a grateful wonder pressed into the service of a plea, that the God who so clothed and fenced a man against every hurt should not now be the one to break the fabric he so carefully raised.
12:
The argument from creation rises from the body to the soul and its sustaining, "Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit," and the witnesses gather up the several gifts the verse names. The reformed John Gill takes "life" first in its natural sense: the quickening in the womb, the rational soul whose presence makes a living man, a grant and a favour that is the chief of mercies, more than meat. But he hears a second life in the word too, the spiritual life given when a man dead in trespasses is quickened by the Spirit of life from Christ, so that Job blesses God at once for his being and for his new being. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the providence: God brought Job from the womb, gave him actual existence, and by his favour furnished the means of life, while "thy visitation," his continual providential care, preserved him in it; for it is by God's unceasing oversight that any man's breath is kept in him, since "in him we live, move, and have our being," the truth Paul owned at Athens in Acts 17:28.

John Wesley unfolds the clauses one by one. God gave not a mere body but a reasonable soul; gave life and then maintained it, in the womb where none could preserve it and afterward through a thousand dangers; added to bare life its many favours, "nourishment by the breast, education, knowledge, and instruction"; and by the care of his providence watched over and visited a life exposed to manifold perils. And Wesley catches the turn on which the whole plea pivots: "Thou hast hitherto done great things for me, and wilt thou now undo all that thou hast done? Shall I, who have been such an eminent monument of thy mercy, now be a spectacle of thy vengeance?"

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sounds the same note of grateful astonishment: the soul is the life, the life is God's gift, and "life is a favour, a great favour, more than meat, more than raiment, a distinguishing favour" that fits us to receive all other favours. Having lighted the lamp of life, Henry says, God does not leave it to burn on its own stock but continually supplies it with fresh oil, so that "thy visitation hath preserved my spirit." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it "Life and favour Thou hast shown me, and thy care hath guarded my breath," closing the recital of mercies. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the high-water mark of Job's remembrance, where the man who elsewhere calls life a burden here calls it favour, and turns every past kindness into a fresh argument that the God who gave and guarded should not now destroy.
13:
The recital of mercies breaks off on a note of foreboding, "And these things hast thou hid in thine heart: I know that this is with thee," and the witnesses divide over whether the hidden thing is God's kindness or his coming stroke. The reformed John Gill weighs the readings and inclines to the darker: "these things" are best understood of the afflictions God had purposed and decreed in his mind, laid up as in a treasury to bring forth in due time, so that even while he formed and favoured Job he had this trouble in reserve. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it the same way and draws out the bitterness of it: Job's sense of God's goodness is embittered by the thought that, while showering good upon him, God "had in reserve for him the trials and sorrows under which he was then labouring," meaning eventually to overwhelm him, and this the very purpose hidden in his heart.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the hidden things more hopefully, as gracious purposes not yet made known: "thou hast had many gracious purposes concerning me which thou hast not made known; but thy visitations and mercy are sufficient proofs of kindness toward me," though for reasons unrevealed thou hast sorely afflicted me and treatest me still as an enemy. John Wesley refuses to choose and takes the phrase to hold both: "both thy former favours and thy present frowns" are hid in God's heart, "both according to thy own will, and therefore undoubtedly consistent, however they seem."

That reconciling instinct the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the whole lesson of the verse. Job could not himself reconcile God's former favours with his present frowns, and so concludes that both are according to the counsel of the same will and must therefore agree, however contrary they look. "When God thus strangely changes his way," Henry writes, "though we cannot account for it, we are bound to believe there are good reasons for it hidden in his heart, which will be manifested shortly"; it is not for us to assign the cause, but with Job we may say, "I know that this is with thee." Known unto God are all his works. So the witnesses circle a real difference, whether the treasure hidden in the divine heart is mercy withheld from sight or judgment held in reserve, yet close on a common confession: that the changing dealings of God spring from one settled and secret purpose, dark to the sufferer now but consistent in the mind of God, and to be owned by faith before it is ever explained.
14:
"If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity." The tone turns from remembrance to a bitter sense of being watched, and the witnesses read the verse as Job's complaint of a justice too strict to bear. The reformed John Gill turns over the sense of "markest me": God took strict notice of his sins, watched their motions and laid them up to bring out against him, or "kept him in" as in a close prison of affliction; and Gill records the further turn of Gussetius, that even if Job had "offered a sacrifice for sin," as certainly he did, it was not regarded, God still marking him and refusing to absolve. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the fear plainly: from God nothing can be hidden, so that if Job sins God takes account of the transgression and "canst not hold me for innocent when thou knowest I am guilty."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the words a charge of summum jus, justice bordering on severity. "If I do but take one false step, misplace a word, or cast a look awry, I shall be sure to hear of it"; conscience, God's deputy, will upbraid him and tell him that every gripe and twitch of pain is the punishment of it. Henry grants the terror of the thought and then relieves it with the gospel's answer: "If God should thus mark iniquities, we should be undone; but we must acknowledge the contrary, that, though we sin, God does not deal in extremity with us." What Job feels as an unsparing scrutiny is not in truth God's way with his own, however it seems under the rod.

The grammatical-historical voices weight the verse toward the whole desperate case it opens. Keil and Delitzsch read the clauses as hypothetical suppositions leading into the next verse, "if I sin," "if I be wicked," "if I be righteous," a man boxed in on every side. Charles Ellicott renders the sequence as one breathless conditional: "If I had sinned Thou wouldst have marked me for punishment, and from mine iniquity Thou wouldst not acquit me; if I had been guilty, woe unto me! and if righteous, I must not lift up my head." The dreadful symmetry, the witnesses agree, is the point: whether Job sins or stands clean, the outcome seems the same, for a watching God marks the one and will not let the other so much as raise his head. The verse states the trap out of which the following lines will cry for release.
15:
The trap of the previous line springs shut here, in the double clause where guilt and innocence come to one dead end, "If I be wicked, woe unto me; and if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head." The reformed John Gill takes the first half at full weight: "if I be wicked, woe is me," in this world and to all eternity, afflictions here and everlasting wrath hereafter, the very portion of a profane and abandoned sinner, or, as the Targum has it, "destruction from the great judgment." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke balances the two halves as a single hopeless equation: if wicked, he must meet the punishment due to iniquity; if righteous, he is only in the state his duty requires and can claim no favour from God's justice, and so, either way, "I am full of confusion," confounded at a lot in which he knows God to be merciful and himself no apostate, yet finds himself treated as though he had departed from all good.

John Wesley reads the two conditions as covering every possibility his friends could name, "wicked," the hypocrite they esteem him, or "righteous," an upright man, "so whether good or bad, all comes to one," for he has no comfort and no hope of any; "confounded within myself, not knowing what to say or do." Out of that confusion he turns the verse into a plea: "Let my extremity move thee to pity, and help me," which is to say, "see thou mine affliction."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses both edges. "A sinful state is a woeful state," he says, and applies it to himself as Job does: "I that have knowledge, that have made a great profession of religion, that was born of good parents; if I be wicked, woe, and a thousand woes, to me." Yet even if righteous, Job "dares not lift up his head," so oppressed and overwhelmed that he cannot look up with any comfort or confidence; without were fightings, within were fears, so that he was "full of confusion" both of face and of spirit, his mind in a constant hurry like the Psalmist who was distracted in Psalm 88:15. Henry hears the closing words as a true prayer breaking through the storm, that God would "see" and take his affliction into compassionate consideration, as David begged him to look upon his affliction and his pain in Psalm 25:18. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott read the same movement, Ellicott paraphrasing the last clause as "I am full of shame; therefore behold Thou mine affliction, for only by Thy taking note of it can I find relief." The witnesses converge: shame has stopped Job's mouth on every side, and his one remaining hope is that the God who seems to watch for his sin might turn the same gaze into pity.
16:
Job's misery is pictured growing of itself and then chased down like prey, "for it increaseth; thou huntest me as a fierce lion," and the witnesses attend both to the obscure opening clause and to the image of the hunting God. The reformed John Gill reads "it increaseth" of the affliction that instead of abating grows upon him, a reason why pity should be shown; the proud waves lift themselves and threaten to overwhelm. He notes too the strange alternative some find in the Hebrew, a wish rather than a statement, "oh that it increased," that the lingering trouble would come at last to its height and quickly make an end of him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the increase plainly, the affliction growing in proportion as it lasted, every day making escape less probable, and then reads the hunting curiously: "as the hunters attack the king of beasts in the forest, so my friends attack me," assailing him on every side, while the God whose designs and works are past finding out "dost both confound and overpower me."

Here a small divergence opens. Where Clarke lets the lion stand for Job hunted by his friends, the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make God himself the lion and Job the quarry: God "huntest me as a fierce lion," as the LORD is the lion of Hosea 5:14, and "wouldst ever anew show Thyself wonderful at my expense." John Wesley reads it the same way and draws out the cruelty of the figure: an ordinary lion "tears its prey speedily, and so ends its torments; but thou renewest my calamities again and again, and makest my plagues wonderful both for kind and extremity and continuance," the marvel being not mercy but a prolonged and astonishing severity.

Charles Ellicott owns the verse "very obscure" and lays out the possibilities without forcing one: it may ask whether it is so glorious a thing that God should hunt him like a lion and then again show himself mysterious toward him, hunting yet hiding both his person and his motive; or the subject may be the lifted-up head of the previous verse, "and if it exalt itself, Thou huntest me"; or, as the Authorized Version takes it, the subject is simply the affliction, "for it increaseth." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the sense: God "showed himself marvellous upon him," making Job a prodigy and a wonder unto many, for all wondered that God would inflict and that Job could bear so much; and what made the affliction most grievous was that he felt God's indignation in it. The witnesses agree on the terror of a God who hunts, and differ only over the grammar of the opening words and whether the lion's pursuit is God's own hand or, with Clarke, the harrying of his friends.
17:
The forensic imagery Job has drawn on all through the speech returns in force, "Thou renewest thy witnesses against me, and increasest thine indignation upon me," and the witnesses part over what those renewed witnesses are. The reformed John Gill takes them not as devils, nor as Job's friends, but as his afflictions, renewed daily and repeated, brought like fresh evidence into a suit that only drags on the longer; or, on another turn, as witnesses against him in the eyes of the world and of his friends, who inferred from his mounting troubles that he must be a wicked man, and read each new stroke as a further proof. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the courtroom cast of the whole passage, where "almost all his terms are forensic": God brings witnesses "in continual succession to confound and convict me," while the last clause, "changes and war," pictures Job assailed by fresh troops, "one company being wearied, another succeeds to the attack, so that I am harassed by continual warfare."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott records the two ways the witnesses have been taken, some understanding the sores on Job's body, which his friends regarded as proofs of his guilt, but Ellicott judging the figure more probably forensic: "Thou still bringest fresh witnesses against me, and multipliest thine anger, so that relays of them, even a host, are against me, host after host, these witnesses of Thine anger, the ministers of Thy vengeance." He pauses over the daring of it: "the sublimity of this indictment against God is only equalled by the sense of terrific awe with which one reads it"; the language is Job's, and so far has the sanction of Holy Writ, yet through it we may learn the condescension as well as the loving-kindness of the Most High, who bears such words from his servant.

John Wesley reads the several terms as one accumulating charge: the witnesses are God's judgments, the evidences at once of Job's sins and of God's wrath; the "indignation" names his miseries as the effects of anger; and in "changes and war" the changes mark the various kinds and the army the great number of his afflictions. Keil and Delitzsch, of the same grammatical-historical school, keep the verse as the hinge into the renewed longing for death that follows. The witnesses do not finally divide over the sense, a man overwhelmed by wave upon wave of trouble that he can only construe as accusation, and differ only over the figure beneath it, whether the fresh witnesses are the afflictions themselves, the sores his friends point to, or the summoned host of a heavenly prosecutor. What none of them softens is the awe of it, that so terrible an arraignment of God should stand in Scripture as the true voice of a suffering saint.
18:
"Wherefore then hast thou brought me forth out of the womb? Oh that I had given up the ghost, and no eye had seen me!" The speech circles back to the wish with which Job first broke silence, and the witnesses mark the relapse with a mixture of blame and compassion. The reformed John Gill rightly ascribes the bringing-forth to God, as the Psalmist did who was taken from the womb by the same hand; and he notes that Job, unmoved by all his friends' reasoning, still holds the mind he was in when he cursed his birth, and "by repeating justifies what he had said," thinking he had cause enough to wish he had died in the womb, since his afflictions only increased and God pursued him as a lion. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts the question as an arraignment of providence itself: "Why didst thou give me a being, when thou didst foresee I should be exposed to such incredible hardships?" sending the reader back to the fuller curse of the third chapter.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the connection, noting that here "Job reverts to the strain of his original curse" in chapter 3; and Keil and Delitzsch read the following clauses as conditionals of what should have been, "I should have expired," the man placing himself back at the moment of birth and mourning the death that mercifully never came.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry feels the fault and yet reaches for its most charitable reading. This is "the language of his passion," a relapse into the very sin he had fallen into before: having just called life a favour in v.12, he now calls it a burden and quarrels with God for laying it on him. But Henry passes on the gentler construction of Caryl, that what troubled Job was to be in a condition that seemed to hinder the great end of his life, the glorifying of God; his harp hung on the willows, out of tune for praise, and he feared his troubles would even reflect dishonour on God and give the enemy cause to blaspheme, so that he wished he had given up the ghost. If that were his meaning, Henry allows, it was still grounded on a mistake, "for we may glorify the Lord in the fires." The witnesses do not divide over the passion of the verse; they only weigh it differently, as impatience that despises the gift of being, or as a zeal for God's honour that has lost its way in grief, and agree that the wish never to have been born is a thing no wish can grant, and a mercy that Job's own later words will outgrow.
19:
Job spells out the painless non-existence he covets, "I should have been as though I had not been; I should have been carried from the womb to the grave," and the witnesses handle the wish with a careful realism. The reformed John Gill will not let the phrase be pressed into a denial of all existence: not that a stillborn child never truly was, but that, comparatively, it is "as if it never had a being," seen by none or few, without a name, without a place in the conversation of men, buried at once and buried in forgetfulness. This, Gill says, is what Job wishes for himself, some even rendering it as an outright longing, "oh that I had been as though I had never been," for then he would have been spared all the sorrows that now surround him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the logic of a merciful oblivion: had Job given up the ghost as soon as born, he could not then have been conscious of existence, so that "as it respects myself, it would have been as though I had never been," the child "immediately transported from my mother's womb to the grave" without ever waking to the misery between. The whole force of the wish lies in that swift passage, birth and burial made almost one act, with no interval of suffering to be remembered.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the verse tightly joined to the plea that follows, the man who wishes he had been carried straight to the grave now turning, in the next breath, to beg a little respite before he goes there in fact. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose comment runs across these verses, hears in the words the extremity of a passion that would rather never have lived than live so; yet he draws from them a sober counsel for the living. We should not be over-fond of life, he says, since even wise and good men have sometimes been brought to complain of it; nor should we inordinately lament the death of infants who are, as this verse has it, as though they had not been, and are carried from the womb to the grave, "when perhaps we ourselves may sometimes wish it had been our own lot." The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the darkest point of Job's longing, where the man reaches past every rank and comfort to envy the child that never drew breath; and they temper it only by reminding the reader that a grief which can make so strange a wish is the measure of how heavy life had grown, not a verdict on the gift of life itself.
20:
From the wish for the grave Job turns to a humbler request, a little ease before the end, grounding it on the shortness of his days: "Are not my days few? cease then, and let me alone, that I may take comfort a little." The reformed John Gill answers the question as self-evidently true: the days of every man are few, and the remainder of Job's, worn as he was by affliction, fewer still; the Hebrew, he notes, may even read "a small little thing," his life no more than a handbreadth, as nothing before God. On that brevity Job builds his plea for respite. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley hears the same argument: "My life is short, and of itself hastens to an end; there is no need that thou shouldest grudge me some ease for so small a moment," the very smallness of the span becoming a reason for a little mercy within it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs both a variant and the daring of the whole cry. He notes a reading that turns the imperative aside from God, "Let him cease, and let me alone," though the sense of a longed-for respite is the same. And he speaks frankly of how near the verge this reply moves: "one cannot but feel that it moves upon the very verge of blasphemy, and is only redeemed therefrom by its pervading reverence and deep undertone of faith." For Job, Ellicott insists, "never gives up his faith in God, though, like Jacob, he wrestles with Him in the dark"; and the issue of the book shows that God is not displeased with such an unburdening of the soul, so long as it keeps close to the straight line of truth.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the prayer tenderly. If Job cannot prevail for the removal of his trouble, he begs at least some intermission, "O let me alone, that I may take comfort a little," some breathing-time, some little enjoyment of himself, which he would reckon a great favour. And the plea "Are not my days few?" Henry says, fastens on the goodness of God's nature, whose consideration is comfortable to an afflicted spirit; those who are not thankful for constant ease should think how welcome one hour's ease would be to a man in constant pain. He turns it back upon the reader too, as an argument to redeem the time: if our days are few, it concerns us to improve them, that we may be ready for the days of eternity that shall be many. The witnesses converge on a prayer at once bold and reverent, a man wrestling in the dark who asks not for vindication now but only for a moment's breath before he goes to the land from which none returns.
21:
The respite Job begs is measured against the finality of where he is going, "before I go whence I shall not return, even to the land of darkness and the shadow of death," and the witnesses read the verse as a sober picture of the grave. The reformed John Gill takes "whence I shall not return" of the passage out of this world to the grave, man's long home, from which there is no coming back to the business and society of life; and he is careful to guard the words from misuse, for Job does not here deny the resurrection, which he elsewhere so strongly asserts, but speaks only of no return to this present life and its affairs, in the same sense he had used before. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in the piled-up phrases the very obscurity of the subject: "I shall not return again from the dust to have a dwelling among men," and the land of darkness is "a place where death rules," over which he projects his shadow, intercepting the light of every kind of life. What, Clarke asks, do we know of the state of separate spirits, or of the spiritual world? and he finds the heaped, uncertain terms an apt confession of our ignorance, pointing the reader back to the shadow of death first named in the third chapter.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the couplet as the threshold of the closing description, the darkness deepening as the sentence runs on. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into a plea and a meditation together. "Lord, give me some ease before I die," he hears Job pray, lest he die of his very pain, as David begged to be lightened lest he sleep the sleep of death in Psalm 13:3. And Henry weighs the state Job so dreads: it is a fixed state, whence we shall not return to live such a life as this, so that we must bid this world a final farewell; and it is, to our natural apprehension, a melancholy one, a land of darkness and the shadow of death. Job, Henry observes, heaps up these expressions to show that he had as dreadful a view of death and the grave as other men naturally have, so that it was only the extremity of his misery that could make him wish for it. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the language of a man driven to long for a rest he still finds fearful, and they quietly set his gloom against the fuller light that his own later faith, and the gospel, would bring to the darkness of the tomb.
22:
"A land of darkness, as darkness itself; and of the shadow of death, without any order, and where the light is as darkness." The chapter closes on a heaping-up of gloom, and the witnesses linger over each stroke of it. The reformed John Gill presses the first phrase to its utmost: it is not merely like darkness but darkness itself, "gross thick darkness, like that of Egypt, that might be felt," the very blackness of darkness, as dark as it can possibly be. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the last, strangest clause, "where the light is as darkness," as a palpable obscure, a place having only such light as renders darkness visible; and he reaches for Sophocles, who has a sufferer cry, "Thou darkness be my light," and for the Vulgate's land of wretchedness and shadow where "no order, but sempiternal horror, dwells," and for Coverdale's blunt English, "wheras is no ordre but terrible feare as in the darknesse."

Clarke will not stop at the picture but turns it to meditation. Here is a duration measured by none of the attributes of time, no order of darkness and light, night and day, summer and winter; it is "the state of the dead, the place of separate spirits," out of time and beyond change, on the very confines of eternity, before whose incomprehensibility he can only stammer the word itself. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the crowded line to the same effect, a land of deep darkness like midnight, of the shadow of death and of confusion, "and which is bright like midnight," the paradox of a light that is itself the thickest dark.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the two great notes of the verse, its disorder and its darkness, and reads each as the negative of a mercy. "There is no order there," he says: perpetual night with no succession of day, all lying on one level, no distinction of prince and peasant, the servant there "free from his master," as an earlier chapter had put it. And "there is no light there": in the grave no knowledge, no comfort, no joy, no praising God, and therefore no light, a darkness that the living, who enjoy the light of life, cannot but fear. Yet Henry lifts one gleam above the gloom: dark as the grave is to man, it is not so to God, for the very dust of the bodies of the saints, though scattered and mingled, is under his eye and shall be forthcoming in the great day. The witnesses close the chapter as Job left it, in a land of ordered nothing where light and darkness are one; but they will not let the last word be the tomb's, reminding the reader that the God whose eye pierces even that darkness is the God who keeps the dust of his own against the morning.
